title: Atlas of Questions · Civilization study
premise: Ideas change what people can explain—and what they can demand from a ruler, a law or a workplace. Keep rival accounts on the desk, follow their documented journeys, and test the distance between a principle and a practice. A separate research successor; the original Atlas and its current journey remain intact.

chapters.completionText: The last page does not describe a perfect civilization. It keeps the instruments, arguments and disagreements that made this world possible—and leaves its people a way to change it.

milestones.title: Copies become evidence
milestones.text: Disagreement between manuscripts can help reconstruct a text. Keep the variants: a finished edition is not the end of transmission.

milestones.title: One sky, more than one surviving model
milestones.text: The phases challenge a strict Ptolemaic arrangement. They do not by themselves choose between every moving- and stationary-Earth alternative.

milestones.title: The past has depth before it has a date
milestones.text: The rocks can establish an ordered, eventful history while its numerical age remains open. This question will return with a new kind of clock.

milestones.title: Kinds become histories
milestones.text: A classification can be reread as a branching history. The mechanism of inheritance is still an unfinished part of the account.

milestones.title: An old question, a new clock
milestones.text: The numerical age is earned through physical decay and solar-system evidence, not supplied by the sequence of strata alone.

milestones.title: The sample leads back to the world
milestones.text: A difficulty in measuring the ancient Earth has exposed a trace of modern industry. A research nuisance has become a public question.

milestones.title: The desk remains open
milestones.text: The future arrangements have not abolished care, disagreement or the cost of decisions. The work ends with a common world still worth arguing about.

sources.note: Primary Nobel lecture; PDF pages 10, 12 and 15 distinguish governed resources from open access and discuss contextual rules, affected-user revision and accountable monitoring; page 22 cautions that groups can fail. sources.note: Primary text, Moyle translation. Natural freedom, slavery, manumission and legal statuses belong to one sixth-century legal compilation.

sources.title: UC Berkeley, The Medieval Law School: manuscripts of Justinian with glosses
sources.note: Collection evidence for Bologna study, marginal interpretation and later circulation of the sixth-century compilation.

sources.title: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)
sources.note: Primary text. Authorization is a covenant among subjects, not a contract signed by the sovereign; the sovereign may be a person or assembly.

sources.title: John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90)
sources.note: Primary text. Consent, majority action, tacit consent and breach of trust are disputed arguments, not a history in which everybody actually consented.

sources.title: Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28
sources.note: Primary document in translation. Abolition, French sovereignty, compulsory agricultural continuity and life governorship coexist.

sources.title: Library of Congress / Bibliothèque Haïtienne des Pères du Saint-Esprit: Laws of Saint-Domingue (1801)
sources.note: Primary printed law collection and archival catalogue; agency and institutions are not reduced to European pamphlets.

sources.title: Haitian Declaration of Independence (1804), Dubois/Garrigus translation
sources.note: Primary declaration; permanent separation from France is not a promise of equal power or an end to coercive labour.

sources.title: BnF, Haiti’s independence debt: archival context, 1794–1922
sources.note: Institutional historical account. Independence in 1804; recognition and coercive indemnity came later, not automatic equal standing.

sources.title: Mémorial de l’abolition de l’esclavage, chronology of abolition
sources.note: Institutional chronology: 1791 uprising, local abolition in 1793, national extension in February 1794. Precise local sequences were not collapsed to one decree.

sources.title: Einstein, Relativity: The Special and General Theory, §§8–9
sources.note: Primary teaching thought experiment. Reception order alone does not establish relative simultaneity; equal midpoint distances and invariant light speed remain required.

notes: Full-length independent Atlas research candidate. The original Atlas scenario, routes and saved-game identities are not modified.

All labels and descriptions are authored paraphrases or clearly marked teaching cases, not historical quotations. Optional Read text is supplementary; combinations must be intelligible from visible labels and descriptions.
Chronology is local to each dated desk. Explicit parallel files and later returns compare overlapping histories without asserting backwards causation.

Connections are separately classified as transmission, adaptation, criticism, teaching-comparison or future-speculation. An item being useful in a modern teaching comparison is not evidence of direct historical influence.
Creation reconstructs an argument, model, objection or object. It does not always certify the truth of the position created; competing explanations and limitations remain available.
The final two desks are authored speculative futures. Their institutions and technologies are proposals, not forecasts or claims of historical inevitability.

No finite-scarcity puzzle, hidden diagram, mental arithmetic, prerequisite lore, automatic creation, repeat-unlock toll or arbitrary end-of-desk culling is intended. Earlier creations are carried only when this desk uses them.

The full In Our Time collection was used privately as research inspiration, not a chapter template. The repository retains only original analysis, bibliographic metadata and source links; temporary BBC abstracts were deleted after mining.

Location successor: stable fixed 390 × 844 reference panels; chapters preserve all objects and arrangement. Sources are comparative reading settings, not a claim that all represented authors met there. Artwork and popup presentation do not certify phone usability.

29 October reading-station successor: four remaining paired desks become honest adjoining workstations, restoring all thirty prior source groups and curated carries. Several comparison desks intentionally exceed ten active manuscripts; this is measured restoration, not a claim that every rich intellectual scene fits the usual small-materials target. Old source leaves and creations remain in scrollback. No recipe, goal, source quotation, or historical save identity is changed.

Civilization successor, 2026-10-29: four connected chapters, documented Roman-law return, optional consent-to-rights route, and a historical freedom-at-work return in the speculative ending. Original/current routes and identities are not edited.
Six procedural combination gates are removed, not represented as arithmetic puzzles: the predecessor already avoided numerical calculation. Rival models, observational checks and limitations remain.
New locations are unillustrated logical-playtest reading desks; no visual/mobile/human enjoyment or publication claim. Existing entry source captions remain unchanged.
Only derivative In Our Time findings and bibliographic metadata were consulted; no BBC abstract corpus was recovered or retained.
